Consult Summary:
- 27-year-old male presented via telehealth minutes after a likely bee/wasp sting to the arm with localized rash and anxiety about breathing; video assessment showed no visible lip/oral swelling or respiratory distress; managed as a localized allergic reaction with antihistamines and safety-net advice.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Difficulty breathing (subjective concern), localized rash at sting site on arm, possible mild right-sided lip swelling sensation, “tongue feels weird,” anxiety.
- Onset/duration: Sting occurred a few minutes prior to consult.
- Course: Symptoms prompted concern; breathing difficulty not “particularly acute.” No prior similar severe reactions.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors: Not discussed.
- Associated symptoms:
  - Positive: Localized redness and puncture mark at sting site; soreness; anxiety/panic symptoms (history of occasional episodes).
  - Negative/pertinent negatives: Patient denies known food, pet allergies. No prior anaphylaxis. No EpiPen use. Doctor did not observe lip swelling or respiratory compromise on video.
- Systems review (as mentioned):
  - Respiratory: Patient reports subjective difficulty breathing; clinician observed normal breathing during call; no stridor reported or observed.
  - Skin: Localized rash/erythema at arm puncture site; no significant swelling per patient; blotchy appearance.
  - ENT: Patient reported lip sensation of swelling on right; clinician did not observe swelling; oral/throat visualization performed without concerning findings.

Past Medical History:
- Eczema (history; no complications mentioned).
- Anxiety/panic attacks (occasional; not on medication).

Medications:
- Current/acute recommendations:
  - Chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet, up to about six times daily.
  - Once-daily antihistamine (specific agent and dose not documented).
- Regular/home medications: Not documented.
- Allergies: Penicillin (allergic).

Social History:
- Occupation: Computer scientist.
- Living situation: Lives alone.
- Pets: Cat at home.
- Tobacco/alcohol/substance use: Not documented.

Family History:
- No known family history of acute allergic reactions or other relevant illnesses reported.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not documented.
- General: Speaking in full sentences; clinician reports breathing appears normal.
- HEENT: Lips “don’t seem swollen” to clinician; intraoral/throat visualization via video without concerning findings; no visible airway compromise.
- Skin: Arm—slight erythema with visible puncture mark; blotchy rash; no significant swelling observed by patient or clinician.
- Respiratory: No stridor; no visible respiratory distress on video.

Investigations:
- None performed or ordered during this consult.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Localized allergic reaction to insect sting (bee vs wasp) with anxiety about potential progression; anaphylaxis considered but not supported by current findings.
  - Plan:
    - Start antihistamine: Chlorphenamine (Piriton) 4 mg tablet, up to ~6 times/day as needed.
    - Alternative: Once-daily antihistamine (specific agent/dose not documented).
    - Safety-net: Seek urgent care/A&E immediately if any signs of anaphylaxis develop (lip/tongue/throat swelling, difficulty breathing, stridor/rasping inspiratory sound, rapid progression of symptoms).
    - Monitor sting site: If redness spreads, area becomes hot/tender, or systemic symptoms suggest infection, re-evaluate; consider antibiotics if infection suspected.
    - Education: Provided information link on anaphylaxis signs/symptoms; advised low threshold to contact clinic if worried.
    - No current indication for allergy testing; consider if recurrent reactions or nonspecific rashes occur.
- Issue 2: Anxiety related to acute event.
  - Plan:
    - Reassurance provided; advised to reach out for support if anxiety worsens or for further guidance.

General Plan items if applicable:
- Follow-up: Return to clinic if symptoms persist, worsen, or recur; immediate emergency care for any airway/breathing concerns.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: Vitals, comprehensive medication reconciliation, detailed ROS, smoking/alcohol/substance history, immunization status not addressed.
- Internal conflicts: Patient reported lip swelling sensation and breathing difficulty; clinician observed no visible lip swelling and normal breathing—conflict noted.
- Transcript quality: Generally clear; some filler/pauses; adequate clinical details captured.
